title: From symmetry to measurable material properties
summary: Connect  primitive cell  displacements, spectral  selection rule , and  physical-property tensor  in a single derivation.
scope: The phonon module treats Γ-point symmetry-adapted displacements and first-order optical selection rules; symmetry alone does not give force constants, phonon frequencies, or actual spectral intensities.
The tensor module derives static equilibrium response forms under specified  point group  constraints. Allowed components can still vanish in a particular material for microscopic reasons.

Si, GaAs and NaCl use ideal cubic structures from the material atlas. Animation amplitudes, spectral peak centers and linewidths are demonstration parameters, not experimental or first-principles data.

sources.title: Bilbao: official SAM help
sources.note: Methodological basis for mechanical representations, Γ-point symmetry-adapted modes, and IR/Raman activity. The site's worked examples, questions, and derivations are original.

sources.title: IUCr：An Introduction to Crystal Physics，Ervin Hartmann
sources.note: Sections 2–4 distinguish tensor transformations, intrinsic index symmetries, and crystal symmetry. Equilibrium and  transport  responses have different applicability conditions.

sources.title: Bilbao: official MTENSOR help
sources.note: Background on tensor constraints from magnetic point groups; this classroom independently derives static linear magnetoelectric response using polar/axial character and time-reversal parity.

sources.title: Etxebarria et al.: Crystal tensor properties of magnetic materials with and without spin–orbit coupling (2025)
sources.note: Illustrates the different regimes of constraints from magnetic point groups and from spin point groups when spin–orbit coupling is neglected. These exercises specify only a magnetic point group; they do not determine the magnetic order of a real material.

sources.title: AFLOW: diamond (A4) structure prototype
sources.note: Verify Si  diamond structure , No.227, and the two-atom  primitive cell .

sources.title: AFLOW: zincblende (B3) structure prototype
sources.note: Verifies GaAs zinc blende, No.216, and inversion absence due to chemically distinct occupations.

sources.title: AFLOW: Rock Salt/Halite (NaCl, B1) structure prototype
sources.note: Check the rock-salt structure of NaCl, No.225, and its two fcc sublattices.

lessons.title: 01 · How do atoms form a vibrational representation?
lessons.summary: Track atomic permutations and displacement directions together at Γ to build the 3N-dimensional mechanical representation.

sections.title: First determine the atom count in the  primitive cell
sections.text: A primitive cell with N atoms has three independent displacements per atom, so its mechanical representation has dimension 3N. The conventional face-centered cubic cells of Si, GaAs and NaCl each contain eight atoms, but their primitive cells contain only two, making this lesson's Γ-point problem six-dimensional. Treating a conventional cell as primitive introduces folded modes; its 24 coordinates cannot simply be identified with six physical phonon branches.

sections.title: One operation does two things
sections.text: A  space group  operation {R|t} first maps site a to a chemically identical site p(a), then rotates displacements with the orthogonal Cartesian matrix R. At Γ, lattice-translation Bloch phases equal 1. The product of atomic permutation matrix P and vector matrix R gives the complete displacement transformation. Nonzero  wavevector  requires translation phases, so this lesson's simplified formula no longer applies.
sections.formula: D_{mech}({R|t}) = P({R|t}) ⊗ R；χ_{mech}(g) = N_{fix}(g) tr R

sections.title: Only atoms returning to their original sites contribute to the trace
sections.text: N_{fix} counts atoms mapped onto themselves modulo primitive translations. Exchanged atoms still move, but their matrix blocks are off-diagonal and contribute no character. For fractional-coordinate input, transform rotations into a Cartesian basis first; fractional axes of an oblique cell are not orthogonal Cartesian axes.

sections.title: Extract  irreducible representation  using inner products
sections.text: Taking character inner products operation by operation over the complete finite point group gives the multiplicity of each irreducible representation. One occurrence of a triply degenerate representation occupies three coordinates: multiplicity and dimension are different quantities. Finally, the dimensions of all components must sum to 3N.
sections.formula: n_α = (1/|G|) Σ_{g} χ_α(g)* χ_{mech}(g)；Σα n_α d_α = 3N

examples.title: Why does inversion give different characters in Si and NaCl?
steps: The Cartesian inversion matrix is −I, with trace −3.
For Si, choosing a bond center as the inversion center exchanges the two basis atoms, so N_{fix}=0.
Na and Cl each return to themselves modulo fcc translations in NaCl, so N_{fix}=2.
Multiplying N_{fix} by −3 gives 0 and −6, respectively.
examples.result: The same point group does not guarantee the same mechanical representation; chemical labels and site occupations matter too.

lessons.title: 02 · separate acoustic and optical modes from six displacements
lessons.summary: Remove the three rigid translations and distinguish symmetry-adapted modes from actual dynamical eigenmodes.

sections.title: For a crystal, subtract the three translations
sections.text: Uniform equal displacements of every atom span the three-dimensional acoustic subspace, transforming as a polar vector at Γ. An infinite periodic crystal does not subtract overall rotations using the isolated-molecule 3N−6 rule; the optical degrees of freedom here number 3N−3.

sections.title: Γ-point decompositions of the three materials
sections.text: Using conventional Oh and Td Mulliken labels, Si has mechanical representation T1u+T2g, NaCl has 2T1u, and GaAs has 2T2. Each material has a three-dimensional acoustic subspace and a three-dimensional optical subspace. T2g is also often written F2g; differing labels do not change the representation dimension.

sections.title: The animation displays symmetry structure
sections.text: Parallel and opposite displacements identify rigid translations and relative motion conveniently. Actual optical motion of unequal-mass atoms generally must satisfy center-of-mass and dynamical constraints; equal-length opposite arrows merely depict a symmetry-adapted basis of relative displacement. Multiple copies of the same  irreducible representation  may also mix through  dynamical matrix .

sections.title: Frequencies require additional physical input
sections.text: Masses and force constants are required to construct a dynamical matrix and calculate frequencies and mass-weighted eigenvectors. In a polar crystal, LO–TO splitting as q→0 also depends on long-range Coulomb terms, Born effective charges, and dielectric response. Γ-point symmetry labels alone cannot determine these values.

examples.title: Do the two T2 copies of GaAs imply six optical branches?
steps: One T2 has dimension 3, so two T2 representations contribute 6 dimensions.
Uniform translations also transform as T2, so subtract one T2 first.
One optical T2 subspace remains, with dimension 3.
examples.result: The two-atom primitive cell of GaAs has three acoustic and three optical branches; identical labels do not make them the same physical subspace.

lessons.title: 03 · why do some modes appear in only one type of spectrum?
lessons.summary: Determine first-order IR and ordinary Raman activity using  polar vector  and symmetric rank-two tensors.

sections.title: Infrared absorption requires linear dipole coupling
sections.text: In the electric-dipole approximation, a mode Q_ν can couple linearly to an electric field only if its representation occurs in the polar-vector representation. This tests whether symmetry forbids coupling; the strength still depends on mode effective charge. Remove uniform acoustic translations before considering optical modes.

sections.title: Ordinary first-order Raman scattering probes changes in polarizability
sections.text: This lesson uses the ordinary first-order, nonresonant Raman approximation with symmetric polarizability. Mode tensors come from the symmetric square Sym²(V), with possible basis functions x²,y²,z²,yz,xz,xy. Resonant magneto-optical processes, antisymmetric scattering terms and higher-order processes require additional assumptions and cannot be classified directly using this table.

sections.title: Inversion imposes even–odd mutual exclusion
sections.text: In an ideal centrosymmetric crystal,  polar vector  is inversion odd, whereas quadratic products are even. A definite-parity Γ-point  optical mode  therefore cannot have both IR and Raman activity as defined here. Mutual exclusion applies to these first-order approximations; it does not mean experimental spectra can never have peaks at the same frequency.

sections.title: Three materials provide a comparison
sections.text: Si optical T2g modes allow Raman scattering but forbid electric-dipole IR absorption. NaCl optical T1u modes allow IR but forbid ordinary first-order Raman scattering. GaAs lacks inversion; T2 transforms both as a vector and as off-diagonal quadratic functions, so both couplings are allowed, although a particular scattering geometry can still give zero signal.

examples.title: Does simultaneous activity in GaAs violate mutual exclusion?
steps: First check that inversion symmetry, the prerequisite for mutual exclusion, is present.
Ga and As cannot be exchanged, so zinc blende lacks the bond-centered inversion of the Si diamond structure.
In Td, both vectors and (yz, xz, xy) transform as T2.
examples.result: The prerequisite does not hold, so the same T2 optical subspace can be both IR- and Raman-active without contradiction.

lessons.title: 04 · rotate polarization to read the Raman tensor
lessons.summary: Derive the angular dependence for parallel and crossed polarizations from scattering amplitudes, distinguishing mode activity from brightness in a particular geometry.

sections.title: Calculate intensity from amplitude first
sections.text: The incident polarization e_{in}, analyzer direction e_{out}, and mode Raman tensor R_ν jointly determine the amplitude. Perform the two matrix contractions before taking the squared modulus; summing squared tensor components cannot replace the amplitude. Here the polarization vectors and model coefficient d are real.

sections.title: Choose a mode component solvable by hand
sections.text: Use crystal axes x,y,z and choose R_z with only xy and yx components equal to d. Light propagates along z and its incident polarization rotates in the xy plane. The parallel analyzer follows e_{in}, while the crossed analyzer is perpendicular to it within the plane. The subscript z merely labels this set of mode-tensor basis functions.

sections.title: The four-lobed angular pattern comes from two contractions
sections.text: The parallel amplitude is 2d sinθ cosθ and the crossed amplitude is d(cos²θ−sin²θ). After normalizing d=1, parallel is dark and crossed bright at θ=0°; the reverse holds at θ=45°. A symmetry-allowed mode can be completely dark in a particular geometry.

sections.title: Line shapes and angular distributions serve different roles
sections.text: The interactive plot can multiply the relative angular intensity by an illustrative line shape with a user-specified center and linewidth. This demonstrates how to read a spectrum; it does not predict a material's actual peak positions. Intensities for different final states are normally added incoherently. Coherent mode superpositions require separately specified phases and preparation.

examples.title: Why is 22.5° a useful consistency check?
steps: Substituting θ=22.5° gives 2θ=45°.
sin²45°=cos²45°=1/2。
Both normalized intensities are 1/2, giving a total of 1.
examples.result: This identity checks the specified R_z and xy polarization geometry; it does not assert identical angular distributions for all Raman tensors.

lessons.title: 05 · How does Neumann's principle become a set of linear equations?
lessons.summary: Apply each symmetry operation to a response tensor to find vanishing components, equal components, and independent parameters.

sections.title: Physical properties must preserve the crystal's existing symmetries
sections.text: For a given equilibrium phase, every crystal point-group operation must preserve its property relations. In P=χE, both P and E are polar vectors, so the second-rank tensor satisfies χ=RχRᵀ. Each operation supplies linear constraints, and their common solution gives the allowed form.
sections.formula: χ_{ij} = Σab R_{ia} R_{jb} χ_{ab}；A vec(χ)=0

sections.title: Intrinsic index symmetries precede crystal constraints
sections.text: This lesson's static equilibrium dielectric response comes from second derivatives of one thermodynamic potential, using χ_{ij}=χ_{ji}. In a linear equilibrium model without couple stresses, the elastic tensor has two minor symmetries and one major symmetry. These conditions are not additional gifts of a crystal system.

sections.title: Cubic symmetry does not make every property isotropic
sections.text: Cubic symmetry reduces the static dielectric tensor to χ0I, leaving one parameter. The same group action on the fourth-rank elastic tensor leaves three independent parameters, C_{11}, C_{12}, and C_{44}. Cubic elasticity is isotropic only if C_{44}=(C_{11}−C_{12})/2 also holds.

sections.title: Rotating a sample does not add a symmetry operation
sections.text: Changing the crystal's experimental orientation transforms the same tensor into laboratory coordinates, multiplying each index by a rotation matrix. Reducing point-group constraints is a different operation: it changes the allowed parameter space. Allowed does not mean actually nonzero, nor does symmetry determine the units, sign or magnitude of material constants.

examples.title: Constrain χ step by step, from C2 to C4
steps: C2(z)=diag(−1,−1,1) equates χ_{xz} and χ_{yz} to their negatives, so they vanish.
Applying C4(z) next makes χ_{xx}=χ_{yy} and sets χ_{xy}=0 for the symmetric tensor.
Here χ_{zz} remains independent. Only after adding a cubic rotation that exchanges z and x do all three diagonal components become equal.
examples.result: Increasing symmetry progressively reduces the number of allowed independent parameters.

lessons.title: 06 · Why is piezoelectricity allowed in GaAs but forbidden in Si and NaCl?
lessons.summary: Derive the zinc-blende piezoelectric form from the sign reversal of a third-rank polar tensor under inversion.

sections.title: First specify which piezoelectric coefficient is being used
sections.text: This lesson uses the strain form P_i=e_ijk ε_jk. Strain ε is symmetric, so e_ijk=e_ikj. Do not confuse e with the d coefficients relating polarization to stress; they are connected through elastic response. Full Cartesian index summation is used below so the factor of two associated with engineering shear is not hidden in notation.

sections.title: Inversion eliminates a third-rank polar tensor
sections.text: Under inversion, polarization changes sign and strain does not. If inversion is a symmetry of the phase, every linear piezoelectric coefficient must equal its negative and vanish. Ideal Si and NaCl are centrosymmetric. Conversely, absence of inversion is only necessary; not all noncentrosymmetric  point group  are piezoelectric groups.

sections.title: Td leaves one independent parameter
sections.text: For the chosen cubic axes, the Td point group of GaAs makes the six e components with three distinct indices equal; all other components vanish. Calling their common value e_0, the complete sum gives P_x=2e_0 ε_{yz}, Py=2e_0 εxz, Pz=2e_0 εxy. Defining engineering shear as γyz=2ε_{yz} gives P_x=e_0γyz.

sections.title: An additional step connects symmetry allowance to material measurements
sections.text: A free parameter means the group does not force it to zero; it supplies neither a value nor a guarantee that every applied strain produces polarization. For example, applying only εxx in the ideal Td model produces no polarization through this linear piezoelectric term, whereas yz shear couples to P_x.

examples.title: Where the shear factor of two comes from
steps: Let ε_{yz}=ε_{zy}=s, with all other strains zero.
The full contraction contains both e_{xyz} ε_{yz} and e_{xzy} ε_{zy}.
Both terms equal e0s, so P_x=2e0s.
examples.result: For e_0=1 and s=1/100, the model gives P_x=1/50. This is a dimensionless demonstration, not measured GaAs polarization.

lessons.title: 07 · How do primed operations constrain magnetoelectric response?
lessons.summary: Treat polar vectors, axial vectors, and time reversal together, and compare inversion i, time reversal 1′, and their composite i′.

sections.title: The static magnetoelectric tensor has distinct inputs and outputs
sections.text: This lesson defines P=αH. P is a time-even polar vector, whereas H is a time-odd axial vector. For a spatial orthogonal matrix R and time factor τ=±1, they transform as RP and τ det(R)RH. Invariance of the constitutive relation then gives the transformation constraint on α.
sections.formula: α = τ det(R) RαRᵀ; τ=−1 denotes an operation with time reversal

sections.title: i and 1′ each forbid α
sections.text: Pure inversion has R=−I and τ=+1, so α=−α. Pure time reversal has R=I and τ=−1, likewise giving α=−α. If either is a symmetry of the magnetic phase, the static linear magnetoelectric term defined here is forbidden.

sections.title: The two minus signs cancel in i′
sections.text: Retaining only the identity and inversion combined with  time reversal , namely i′, gives τ=−1 and det(R)=−1, so the constraint becomes α=α. This single nontrivial operation therefore leaves all nine components unrestricted. Additional spatial or magnetic operations can reduce the freedom further. α need not be symmetric; equilibrium reciprocity connects direct and converse magnetoelectric responses rather than imposing α_{ij}=αji arbitrarily.

sections.title: Specify the magnetic phase before discussing a material
sections.text: The i′ exercise is an explicitly specified two-element magnetic point-group model; it does not assert that any material necessarily belongs to it. Actual magnetic order, domains, external fields, and spin–orbit coupling affect the applicable symmetry group. Transport, dissipative optics, and spin groups without spin–orbit coupling require their own physical transformation rules; the static formulas in this lesson do not apply directly.

examples.title: Three models differing by a single switch
steps: With generator i, the allowed space has dimension 0.
Set the generator to 1′: the allowed space still has dimension 0.
Set  generator  to i′: considering only this  generator  leaves an allowed space of dimension 9.
examples.result: A prime does more than rename an ordinary point group: it changes the constraint sign for time-odd responses.

lessons.title: 08 · Complete a reproducible derivation using one material
lessons.summary: Confirm the model in the material atlas, make predictions in the lesson, then use the same material in  phonon  and tensor calculations.

sections.title: Step 1: fix the model and coordinates
sections.text: Open the material atlas and record the phase, space group, chemical occupations, and chosen crystal axes. These examples all use ideal cubic structures. Defects, surfaces, strain, or magnetic order that changes symmetry requires a new model. Keeping the material ID during calculation, rather than only a group name, helps avoid confusing the vibrational representations of Si and NaCl.

sections.title: Step 2: make a testable prediction first
sections.text: First determine the primitive-cell atom count and mechanical representation, subtract acoustic translations, and classify optical activity. Then choose a property tensor and predict its independent parameters and zero components. Record selection rules, allowed forms, demonstration parameters and unknown material constants separately.

sections.title: Step 3: change one experimental condition
sections.text: Keep the material fixed while changing mode components and polarization angles in the  phonon  demonstration, or fields, strain, and sample orientation in the tensor demonstration. Check a special angle, a forbidden component, or a shear response by hand to detect coordinate and factor-of-two errors promptly.

sections.title: Step 4: save the inputs and the scope of your conclusion
sections.text: Save the material, preset, tensor type, directions, coefficients, and output. Identical inputs should reproduce the same symmetry result. Comparison with experimental frequencies, absolute intensities, or material constants requires their sources, temperatures, units, and measurement or calculation conditions.

examples.title: Compare three materials with the same two-atom  primitive cell  at a glance
steps: Si: T2g optical modes, ordinary Raman allowed, electric-dipole IR forbidden, and zero linear piezoelectricity.
NaCl: the T1u optical mode is IR allowed and forbidden in ordinary first-order Raman scattering; linear piezoelectricity vanishes.
GaAs: T2  optical mode , both IR and Raman allowed; the Td piezoelectric form has one free parameter.
examples.result: The same primitive-cell atom count guarantees only the same number of degrees of freedom; site occupations, chemical labels and the group action determine physical selection rules.

exercises.title: Derive the characters of the mechanical representation step by step
exercises.prompt: At Γ, an operation returns both atoms to their own positions modulo  primitive cell  translations. The spatial operation is a 180° rotation about z. Find the  character  of  mechanical representation , then compare with the case in which the atoms are exchanged.

steps.prompt: What is the trace of the Cartesian matrix for C2(z)?
steps.hint: x and y reverse; z is unchanged.
steps.explanation: diag(−1,−1,1) has trace −1.

steps.prompt: What is χ_{mech} when both atoms return to themselves?
steps.hint: Multiply N_{fix} by the matrix trace.
steps.explanation: χ_{mech}=2×(−1)=−2; do not multiply by the group order.

steps.prompt: What is χ_{mech} if the operation exchanges the two atoms?
steps.hint: The exchange blocks lie off the main diagonal.
steps.explanation: N_{fix}=0, so  character  is 0; this does not mean the operation acts trivially.

steps.prompt: What character should the identity operation give as a dimension check?
steps.hint: Each atom has three displacement coordinates.
steps.explanation: χ(E)=dim Γ_{mech}=3N=6。

exercises.title: Extract the optical subspace from GaAs 2T2
exercises.prompt: GaAs has two atoms per primitive cell, mechanical representation 2T2, and dim(T2)=3; rigid translations also transform as T2.

steps.prompt: What is the total dimension of the mechanical representation?
steps.hint: Multiply  multiplicity  by the dimension of  irreducible representation .
steps.explanation: 2×3=6, equal to 3N for two atoms.

steps.prompt: Which term should be subtracted from Γ_{mech}?
steps.hint: An infinite periodic crystal has three rigid translations at Γ.
steps.explanation: Subtract the acoustic vector representation T2; 3N−6 is the counting rule for an isolated nonlinear molecule.

steps.prompt: How many optical degrees of freedom remain?
steps.hint: Do not count one T2 representation as one coordinate.
steps.explanation: Γ_{opt}=T2, with dimension 3.

steps.prompt: What conclusion follows from this decomposition alone?
steps.hint: Distinguish symmetry classification from dynamical numerical values.
choices: Obtain actual LO and TO frequencies
It gives mode symmetry types; frequencies still require dynamical input
The measured intensities of all three optical modes must be equal
steps.explanation: Symmetry gives the subspace structure; frequencies and intensities require force constants, effective charges, and other inputs.

exercises.title: Derive the spectral difference between Si and NaCl using parity
exercises.prompt: In Oh, the polar vector transforms as T1u and the symmetric second-rank tensor decomposes as A1g+E_g+T2g. Optical representations are T2g for Si and T1u for NaCl. Use the electric-dipole IR and ordinary first-order Raman approximations.

steps.prompt: What type of activity does the Si T2g optical mode have?
steps.hint: Check separately whether the vector and symmetric rank-two tensor contain T2g.
steps.explanation: T2g occurs in the symmetric second-rank tensor but not in the polar-vector representation T1u.

steps.prompt: What type of activity does the NaCl T1u optical mode have?
steps.hint: g and u denote different inversion parities.
steps.explanation: T1u transforms as a polar vector but is absent from the symmetric second-rank tensor above, whose components all have even parity.

steps.prompt: Why can GaAs T2 be active in both?
steps.hint: First check the prerequisite for inversion-based mutual exclusion.
choices: Because every triply degenerate mode is active in both
Because Td lacks inversion, and both vectors and off-diagonal quadratic functions contain T2
Because GaAs does not need its acoustic modes subtracted
steps.explanation: The absence of inversion removes mutual exclusion, but each representation must still be checked. Absence of inversion alone does not make every mode active.

steps.prompt: After observing an experimental Raman signal in NaCl, what is the correct next step?
steps.hint: The conclusion is restricted to ordinary first-order processes in the ideal structure.
choices: Immediately rule out the space group
Check experimental conditions such as higher-order processes, defects, surfaces or changed symmetry
steps.explanation: First-order selection rules do not exclude every other scattering mechanism or directly diagnose an experimental sample.

exercises.title: Calculate one polarization scan by hand
exercises.prompt: Given R_z=[[0,1,0],[1,0,0],[0,0,0]] and e_{in}=(cosθ,sinθ,0), the crossed analyzer direction is (−sinθ,cosθ,0). Calculate relative intensities from squared amplitudes.

steps.prompt: What is the parallel-polarization amplitude?
steps.hint: Calculate e_{in}ᵀR_z e_{in}.
steps.explanation: The two nonzero terms sum to 2sinθcosθ=sin2θ.

steps.prompt: What is (I∥,I⊥) at θ=0°?
steps.hint: The crossed amplitude is cos2θ.
steps.explanation: sin²0=0，cos²0=1。

steps.prompt: What is (I∥,I⊥) at θ=22.5°?
steps.hint: Here 2θ=45°.
steps.explanation: sin²45°=cos²45°=1/2。

steps.prompt: The parallel geometry gives zero at θ=0°. What does this mean?
steps.hint: Distinguish group-theoretic activity from the actual tensor contraction.
choices: The mode is forbidden in every optical process
The mode tensor contracts to zero in this geometry
steps.explanation: A dark signal caused by geometry does not imply that the mode is absent or has zero frequency.

exercises.title: Reduce the static dielectric tensor step by step
exercises.prompt: Start with a real symmetric 3×3 dielectric response χ, apply C2(z), then C4(z), and finally a 120° cubic rotation about [111].

steps.prompt: Which components does C2(z) force to vanish?
steps.hint: Matrix entry χ_{ij} multiplied by R_{ii}R_{jj}.
choices: χ_{xz}, χ_{yz}, and their symmetric counterparts
steps.explanation: xz and yz acquire one minus sign; xy acquires two and is therefore not forbidden by this operation.

feedback.message: A diagonal entry acquires the square of the sign associated with its direction, so this operation does not reverse its sign.

remediation.prompt: Under a reflection that reverses only x, what factor multiplies χxx?
remediation.explanation: Each x index contributes −1, giving a product of +1.

feedback.message: χxy acquires two minus signs. One reversed coordinate does not by itself imply that this component changes sign.

remediation.prompt: Under C2(x)=diag(1,−1,−1), what is the transformation factor for χyz?
remediation.explanation: Each of y and z contributes −1, giving a product of +1.

feedback.message: One z index and one transverse index contribute a single minus sign; invariance requires these components to vanish.

steps.prompt: How many independent parameters remain after adding C4(z)?
steps.hint: χ_{xx}=χ_{yy} and χ_{xy}=0, while χ_{zz} may still differ.
steps.explanation: The allowed form is diag(a, a, c), with two parameters.

feedback.message: A rotation about z interchanges transverse directions; it does not interchange z with x or y.

remediation.prompt: Is diag(4,4,7) invariant under a 90° rotation about z?
remediation.explanation: The two transverse coefficients must agree; the coefficient along z may differ.

feedback.message: The fourfold rotation also removes the transverse off-diagonal component and equates the transverse diagonal entries. The z direction retains its own coefficient.
Apply the newly added rotation constraint as well, rather than stopping at the previous step.

remediation.prompt: A 90° rotation transforms [[a,b],[b,c]] into [[c,−b],[−b,a]]. If the matrix is invariant, can b vary freely?
remediation.explanation: b=−b requires b=0; a=c is also required.

steps.prompt: What form is allowed after additionally cycling x→y→z→x?
steps.hint: Check how the z diagonal component relates to the x and y diagonal components.
steps.explanation: All three diagonal components must be equal, leaving one independent parameter.

feedback.message: The cyclic operation connects all three directions, equating the diagonal coefficients left by the first two steps.
Index symmetry does not imply invariance under every crystal operation.

remediation.prompt: After cyclically permuting the three axes of diag(2,2,5) once, is the matrix unchanged?
choices: Every real symmetric matrix is invariant
remediation.explanation: The 5 moves to another axis. A matrix being real symmetric does not establish crystal invariance.

feedback.message: Equivalent directions must have equal responses; the response is not restricted to a single axis.

remediation.prompt: Is qI with q≠0 forbidden by a cyclic permutation of the axes?
choices: Yes; all three diagonal entries must be 0
remediation.explanation: Three equal diagonal entries remain equal after permutation. Nonzero q is not forbidden.

steps.prompt: Does this mean cubic elasticity also has only one parameter?
steps.hint: Elasticity is a fourth-rank tensor, so its constraint space is different.
choices: Yes; all cubic material properties are isotropic
No; it generally retains the three parameters C_{11}, C_{12}, and C_{44}
No; there are normally 81 independent parameters
steps.explanation: Fourth-rank elasticity retains three independent parameters after imposing intrinsic index symmetries and cubic constraints.

feedback.message: Second-rank dielectric and fourth-rank elastic tensors have different component spaces. Their parameter counts cannot be transferred directly.

remediation.prompt: Do C11=10, C12=4, and C44=2 satisfy the isotropy condition C44=(C11−C12)/2?
choices: Cubic symmetry makes the check unnecessary
remediation.explanation: The right-hand side is 3, not the given 2. Cubic symmetry does not enforce this additional relation.

feedback.message: For the equilibrium linear elasticity considered here, intrinsic index symmetries and cubic constraints together leave three independent parameters.
81 is the number of entries in a general four-index array, before imposing any index or crystal symmetries.

remediation.prompt: Under the minor symmetries of equilibrium linear elasticity, how are Cxyxy and Cyxxy related?
choices: must be opposites of each other
remediation.explanation: Exchanging the first pair of indices leaves the coefficient unchanged, so some array entries are already dependent.

exercises.title: Derive GaAs piezoelectricity while retaining the shear factor of two
exercises.prompt: In the Td model, all e_{ijk} with three distinct indices equal e_0 and all other components vanish. Set e_0=1 and ε_{yz}=ε_{zy}=1/100, with every other strain zero, and use the full contraction P_i=Σjk e_{ijk} ε_{jk}. All numbers are dimensionless demonstration values.

steps.prompt: How many nonzero contributions enter P_x?
steps.hint: Write j=y,k=z and j=z,k=y separately.
steps.explanation: e_{xyz}ε_{yz} and e_{xzy}ε_{zy} each contribute e_0/100.

steps.prompt: What value of P_x does the calculation give?
steps.hint: Do not omit the second symmetric strain component.

steps.prompt: What is the relation in terms of engineering shear γyz=2ε_{yz}?
steps.hint: The factor of two is already included in γyz.
steps.explanation: P_x=2e_0ε_{yz}=e_0γyz; do not multiply by 2 again.

steps.prompt: What is the linear piezoelectric contribution for the same strain in ideal centrosymmetric Si?
steps.hint: A third-rank polar tensor changes sign under inversion.
choices: Determined solely by the Si atomic mass
steps.explanation: Inversion requires e=−e, so the entire linear piezoelectric tensor vanishes. Other mechanisms, such as nonuniform strain gradients, are outside this discussion.

exercises.title: Compare the constraints of i, 1′, and i′ on α
exercises.prompt: Consider only static P=αH with α=τdet(R)RαRᵀ. Use i,1′ or i′ in turn as the sole nontrivial generator, without other constraints; α is not assumed symmetric.

steps.prompt: What relation does pure inversion i impose?
choices: α=α, so there are nine parameters
It only requires α to be symmetric
steps.explanation: The −I factors on both sides cancel, but the axial factor detR still contributes a minus sign.

steps.prompt: What relation follows from pure time reversal 1′?
choices: α is an arbitrary symmetric matrix
steps.explanation: P is time-even and H is time-odd, so the static linear magnetoelectric coefficient is time-odd.

cases.name: Si: observe Raman activity and check vanishing piezoelectricity
cases.summary: Use the same diamond-structure model to connect 3D displacements, polarization selection rules and inversion-forbidden linear piezoelectricity.
cases.phase: Ideal diamond structure, Fd-3m (No.227), point group m-3m (Oh), two-atom primitive cell.
cases.question: For the specified R_z, d=1, xy parallel polarization, and θ=45° model, what is the relative Raman intensity? How many free linear piezoelectric parameters does the same ideal structure have?
cases.answer: The relative Raman intensity is sin²90°=1. Inversion forces the linear piezoelectric tensor to zero, leaving 0 free parameters.
limitations: The Raman tensor coefficient d=1 is a normalized demonstration parameter, not the measured polarizability derivative of silicon.
These conclusions apply to ordinary first-order Raman,  electric dipole  IR, and linear piezoelectricity in ideal bulk crystals, excluding surface, defect, and higher-order mechanisms.

cases.name: GaAs: from an optical mode active in both probes to shear piezoelectricity
cases.summary: Chemical occupation removes inversion, allowing the T2 optical mode in both IR and Raman scattering and leaving one piezoelectric coefficient.
cases.phase: Ideal  zinc blende  structure, F-43m（No.216）,  point group  -43m（Td）, two-atom  primitive cell .
cases.question: With e_0=1, ε_{yz}=ε_{zy}=1/100 and every other strain zero, what polarization vector does the Td model give? Which first-order optical couplings are allowed for this material's T2 optical modes?
cases.answer: P=(1/50,0,0), because the complete sum includes two shear components. T2 is allowed in both electric-dipole IR and ordinary first-order Raman scattering, although particular polarization geometries can still give zero signal.
limitations: Shear and coefficient values are dimensionless model inputs, not measured GaAs piezoelectric constants.
Equal-amplitude opposite displacements illustrate only a symmetry basis for relative motion; physical optical eigenvectors with unequal atomic masses require dynamical input.
Γ-point labels do not determine LO–TO splitting or frequencies.

cases.name: NaCl: infrared activity and forbidden first-order Raman scattering
cases.summary: Compare different atomic permutations within the same Oh point group as Si to understand T1u optical modes and inversion constraints.
cases.phase: Ideal rock-salt structure, Fm-3m (No.225), point group m-3m (Oh), two-atom primitive cell.
cases.question: What is NaCl's inversion mechanical  character ? After removing acoustic translations, what are the optical subspace dimension and first-order IR/Raman activities?
cases.answer: Inversion preserves both atoms' own sites, so χ_{mech}(i)=2×(−3)=−6. The optical subspace is three-dimensional T1u: electric-dipole IR is allowed and ordinary first-order Raman is forbidden.
limitations: Being forbidden in ordinary first-order Raman scattering does not imply zero Raman signal at every order or in every defective sample.
Actual infrared oscillator strengths and LO–TO splitting require effective charges, dielectric response, and dynamical data.
